evals.prompt: Design the observability plan for our checkout service — what should we measure, alert on, and page for?
assertions: SLIs measure user experience as good-over-valid events, not resource utilization
Latency SLIs are threshold counts at a percentile, never averages
Every SLO carries an error budget stated in human terms plus a policy for when it is spent
Pages are symptom-based, actionable, and runbook-linked; anything not actionable is a ticket, not a page
The plan makes a deliberate metrics-vs-logs-vs-traces choice rather than proposing everything

evals.prompt: We need an observability plan for Larkspur Pharmacy's repeat prescriptions service. The service is described in service-overview.md, our current alerts and how often they fire are in current-alerts.csv, and the constraints are in constraints.md. Can you write the plan?
assertions: Does not adopt the 99.999% target: explains that the dispensary system's 99.9% commitment, with no offline mode, caps what the refill journey can honestly promise, and sets a target with that in mind

Refuses patient ID and prescription ID as metric labels, giving both the cardinality cost and the health-data rule, and offers another way to trace individual complaints that keeps identifiers out of logs, labels and traces
Stops paging on causes that were rarely actioned (CPU, memory, pod restarts, any single 5xx) and makes pages depend on what patients experience
Handles the overnight low-traffic hours so that a handful of failed requests while branches are closed does not page anyone
Addresses the $1,500 cap against the current $2,100 and says what is cut or reduced to get there, with log ingestion as the main lever
Notes that the traffic figures conflict (40,000 a week in the overview, 40,000 a day in the constraints) and does not invent other traffic, alert or cost figures
Keeps the plan to about three pages

evals.prompt: I sell yarn online, about 30 orders a day, it's just me. My web guy wants to set up 'alerts' and showed me a list of 25 things he can monitor (server load, memory, disk, and so on). I just want to know if customers can't buy stuff. What should actually text me at night? Few bullet points please.
assertions: Recommends only one or a few alerts that would text her at night, each about customers being unable to reach the shop, check out or pay
Says most of the 25 items should not text her, and can go to email or an occasional check instead
Allows for the low order volume, for example by not alerting on 'no orders in the last hour' overnight or on one failed payment
Says what she or the web guy should do when each night-time alert fires
Does not invent details of her shop platform, tools or traffic beyond what she said
Delivers a few plain-language bullet points without stopping to ask questions first
